# Exact cubic ear potential at every tight strict-incidence triangle

This note gives a necessary and sufficient scalar criterion for every
first-order outward ear on one edge of a cubic-tight triangle to have
nonpositive cubic derivative. Sections 4--6 prove that criterion STRICTLY
for every such triangle, including asymmetric cubic equality cases.
Unlike separate raw-area variations, it retains the actual section changes
and the full geometric tent along the edge. No finite-ear assertion follows.

## 1. Setting and shape derivative

Let T have strict distinct-vertex cap incidence at an interior source, and
suppose its ordinary cubic functional Psi=sum f_i^2+prod f_i equals 4.
Fix one edge P_i P_j, opposite vertex P_s. Parameterize it by
P(t)=(1-t)P_i+tP_j, 0<=t<=1. Write

    a=the parameter where cap j begins,
    b=the parameter where cap i ends.

Then 0<a<b<1. Indeed the edge has negative margin for cap s everywhere;
since the three balanced margins sum to zero, caps i and j overlap rather
than leaving a gap along that edge. In terms of signed vertex margins,

    a=(-v_j.(P_i-y))/[v_j.(P_j-P_i)],
    b=v_i.(P_i-y)/[v_i.(P_i-P_j)].

Choose the outward vector w equal to the outward ninety-degree rotation
of P_j-P_i divided by |P_j-P_i|^2. Thus the coordinates P(t)+r w have
area Jacobian one. The first variation under a continuous piecewise-affine
outward roof r=epsilon h(t), with h(0)=h(1)=0, is a linear functional

    D Psi[h]=integral h(t) dnu(t).                    (1)

Here nu has a piecewise constant density and possible point masses only
at a,b. The density is

    alpha_i on (0,a),
    beta_s  on (a,b),
    alpha_j on (b,1),                                (2)

where alpha_i is the derivative for adding raw area simultaneously to
k and Q_i with all sections fixed, and beta_s is the derivative for
adding raw area to k,Q_i,Q_j with sections fixed. They are exactly the
coefficients in
`candidate 7a495c3fafcaeba9`.

To justify (1)--(2), the area derivatives are the integrals of h over
the corresponding fixed-signature intervals. A cutting line intersects
the edge transversely at a or b. Its first section-length derivative is
a fixed multiple of h at that intersection, producing a point mass.
The displacement of a clipping intersection by O(epsilon) changes the
area integral only by O(epsilon^2) for a fixed Lipschitz roof. Thus no
extra density or boundary term occurs. The same formula also applies to
affine roofs induced by moving either edge endpoint; their adjacent
edge contributions must then be included.

## 2. The two edge moments vanish separately

The cubic of every nearby strict-incidence triangle is at most 4, while
it equals 4 at T. It is a differentiable function of its three vertex
coordinates there, so all of its vertex derivatives vanish.

Moving vertex P_i creates affine normal roofs on its two adjacent edges.
The two scalar normal displacements may be chosen independently because
their edge normals are linearly independent. The roof on P_i P_j is a
constant multiple of 1-t. Therefore its coefficient vanishes separately.
Repeating at P_j gives the second identity:

    integral (1-t) dnu(t)=0,
    integral t dnu(t)=0.                             (3)

This argument uses actual triangle variations and their exact cubic bound.
It does not assume the ear itself is a triangle variation.

## 3. Exact Green potential for every peak

For 0<theta<1 put

    G(t,theta)=min(t,theta)-t theta,
    U(theta)=integral G(t,theta) dnu(t).

The unit-height triangular roof with peak theta is
G(t,theta)/[theta(1-theta)], so its cubic derivative has the sign of U.
Distributionally U''=-nu. In addition U(0)=U(1)=0, while (3) gives
U'(0)=U'(1)=0. Consequently (2) yields the exact outer formulas

    U(theta)=-alpha_i theta^2/2,       0<=theta<=a,
    U(theta)=-alpha_j(1-theta)^2/2,    b<=theta<=1.     (4)

For theta=a+z(b-a), 0<=z<=1, the middle formula is

    2U(theta)=-(1-z)alpha_i a^2-z alpha_j(1-b)^2
                              +beta_s(b-a)^2 z(1-z). (5)

It follows by matching the endpoint values in (4) and using U''=-beta_s
on the middle interval. Thus all point-mass effects, including actual
section changes, are already exactly incorporated in (4)--(5).

At a positive cubic boundary every alpha_i is strictly positive, by the
completed-square estimate in the global unique-loss theorem. Hence all
unique-tip ears have strictly negative derivative. All middle-tip ears
have nonpositive derivative if and only if

    beta_s(b-a)^2
       <=[a sqrt(alpha_i)+(1-b)sqrt(alpha_j)]^2.      (6)

For beta_s<=0 this is automatic. Otherwise divide (5) by z(1-z), and use

    min_(0<z<1) [A/z+B/(1-z)]=(sqrt(A)+sqrt(B))^2

with A=alpha_i a^2 and B=alpha_j(1-b)^2. This proves both directions
of (6). Strict inequality gives a strict derivative for every interior
peak; equality identifies the unique possible zero peak.

The inequality (6) is the exact coupled first-variation target at a
general cubic-tight triangle. In particular a positive raw beta_s, such
as the actual two-ceiling example in the cited note, is not a counterexample
to the cubic: it must pay the two neighboring corner and section costs
visible in (6). We now prove (6) strictly using the actual equality data.

## 4. A disk inequality with a complete endpoint proof

Let 0<U,V<1, L=U+V-1>0, 0<F<1, and 0<=r<=F(1-F). Put

    A(r)=[(U-F)^2+r]/U^2,
    B(r)=[(V-1+F)^2+r]/V^2.

Then

    [(1-V)sqrt(A(r))+(1-U)sqrt(B(r))]^2
                         > L^2[A(r)+B(r)-1].          (7)

Define the gap between these sides to be J(r). Its nonradical terms are
affine in r. Its only nonlinear term is
2(1-U)(1-V)sqrt(A(r)B(r)), which is concave: for positive affine
A=a+br and B=c+dr the second derivative of sqrt(AB) is
-(ad-bc)^2/[4(AB)^(3/2)]<=0. Cases with a zero endpoint follow by
continuity. Thus J is concave on the stated closed interval. It suffices
to prove positivity at its two endpoints.

At r=F(1-F), write A=A(r), B=B(r) and

    Z=(1-V)^2 A+(1-U)^2 B-L^2(A+B-1).

Direct expansion gives the exact identities

    Z=-2(U-1)(V-1)[FU-FV+UV-U]/(UV),

    Z^2-4(1-U)^2(1-V)^2 AB
       =-4F(1-F)(1-U)^2(1-V)^2 L^2/(U^2 V^2)<0.     (8)

Hence Z+2(1-U)(1-V)sqrt(AB)>0, whether Z is positive or negative.
This is J(r)>0 at that endpoint.

At r=0 introduce the signed roots

    z_1=(U-F)/U,      z_2=(V-1+F)/V.

They satisfy z_1,z_2<=1 and U z_1+V z_2=L>0, so they cannot both
be negative. If both are nonnegative, then

    1=U(1-z_1)+V(1-z_2)<(1-z_1)+(1-z_2),

because U,V<1 and the two nonnegative summands cannot both vanish.
Thus z_1+z_2<1 and z_1^2+z_2^2-1<0; (7) follows strictly.

Otherwise, by interchanging U,V and replacing F by 1-F if necessary,
write z_1=-t<0 and z_2=b>0. Then

    L/V<=b<=1,       t=(Vb-L)/U.

The proposed right root is
R=(1-V)t+(1-U)b. The difference R-Lt is affine in b. At its interval
endpoints its values are respectively

    (1-U)L/V>0,       2(1-U)(1-V)/U>0.

Therefore R>Lt throughout. Since t^2+b^2-1<=t^2, this gives
R^2>L^2(t^2+b^2-1), again exactly (7). This proves the other endpoint.
Concavity now proves (7) on the entire interval.

## 5. Exact substitution of a cubic-tight triangle

Normalize its three positive vertex margins to sum one. Write them a_i
and put L_ij=v_i.(P_i-P_j)/H, where H is the unnormalized sum of the
positive margins. Cyclically label the edge under discussion as (i,j)
and the omitted vertex as s, and abbreviate

    p=L_ij, q=L_ji, D=p+q-2pq.

The strict triangle cube coordinates give 0<p,q<1. Cubic equality is
the detailed-balance cycle identity. Solving that identity for the third
cube coordinate gives

    F=p(1-q)/D,       G=q(1-p)/D,       F+G=1,

    f_i^2=4p^2(1-q)/D,
    f_j^2=4q^2(1-p)/D,
    f_s^2=4(1-p)(1-q).

In particular, with P=f_i f_j f_s, C=8+P and E_i=2f_i^2+P,

    P=8pq(1-p)(1-q)/D,
    C=8(p+q-pq)(1-pq)/D,
    E_i/C=p(1-q)/(1-pq),
    E_j/C=q(1-p)/(1-pq).                             (9)

Now put

    U=a_i/p,       V=a_j/q,
    r=F G (1-p)(1-q)/(1-pq).

The edge intersections in Section 1 are a=1-V and b=U. Thus
0<U,V<1 and L=b-a=U+V-1>0. Also 0<r<FG because
(1-p)(1-q)<1-pq, the difference being D>0.

For each triangle vertex cap, T_i=sqrt(k/Q_i)=f_i/(2a_i). Substituting
this and (9) into the exact unique-area derivative yields

    alpha_i/(C/(2k))=[(U-F)^2+r]/U^2=A(r),
    alpha_j/(C/(2k))=[(V-G)^2+r]/V^2=B(r).            (10)

For transparency, the first identity expands to

    1+(E_i/C) f_i^2/(4a_i^2)-f_i^2/(2a_i)
        =[(U-F)^2+r]/U^2;

all denominators are positive. The second is obtained by interchanging
p,q and F,G. The double-area derivative is exactly

    beta_s=alpha_i+alpha_j-C/(2k),                    (11)

because it adds both cap areas but adds the total area only once.

Multiplying the disk inequality (7) by C/(2k)>0 and using
a=1-V, 1-b=1-U, and (10)--(11) proves (6) STRICTLY.

## 6. Actual local conclusion and scope

For every strict distinct-vertex cubic-tight triangle, every nonzero
outward triangular ear whose peak lies in the relative interior of any
edge has strictly negative first derivative of Psi. This includes all
unique-tip and all double-tip locations and the two cut-crossing peak
positions. No symmetry, cap ceiling, or profile condition is needed.

The proof is an actual geometric first variation: its nu includes both
changed cap areas and the changed cutting sections. A positive raw
double-area derivative can occur, but its actual neighboring loss and
section terms are paid by (7).

For a fixed triangle and a compact set of peak parameters away from its
vertices, continuity gives a uniform negative first-variation margin.
Peaks approaching vertices require a separate uniform remainder argument,
and finite ears or arbitrary quadrilaterals require a separate continuation
or extremal argument. Neither is asserted in this note.
